mockText: 45 items in 50 minutes, with 4 hands-on items (logs, terminal, ordering, diagram), flags and a review screen. Cisco doesn't publish the real item count or the topic weights, so this is a stand-in that fits the real 50 minutes, with an even mix across the five domains.
lead: Cisco's entry-level security cert. It proves you know what a junior analyst or help desk tech needs: core security ideas, how networks and endpoints get attacked and protected, vulnerability and risk basics, and how incidents are handled. Cisco calls it a first step toward CCNA Cybersecurity.
objSub: Five topic areas from Cisco's 100-160 exam topics. Tick objectives as you study them; progress saves on this device.

cur.label: Current exam
cur.note: One 50-minute exam. Cisco doesn't publish a question count or a passing score; you get a pass/fail report when you finish. Test at a Pearson VUE center, online, or at a school's Certiport testing center.
cur.onote: Cisco numbers these topics but doesn't publish weights. The bars split study time evenly across the five areas.

domains.name: Essential Security Principles
obj: Define core security principles
Threats, vulnerabilities, exploits and risk; attack vectors; hardening; defense in depth; CIA; attacker types and motives; code of ethics.
Explain common threats and vulnerabilities
Malware, ransomware, DoS, botnets, social engineering, physical attacks, man-in-the-middle, IoT flaws, insiders and APTs.
Explain access management
AAA, RADIUS, multifactor authentication and password policies.
Explain encryption and where it's used
Encryption types, hashing, certificates and PKI, strong vs weak algorithms, data at rest and in transit, secure protocols.

domains.name: Basic Network Security Concepts
obj: Describe TCP/IP protocol weaknesses
TCP, UDP, HTTP, ARP, ICMP, DHCP and DNS.
Explain how addressing affects security
IPv4 and IPv6, MAC addresses, segmentation, CIDR, NAT, public vs private networks.
Describe network security infrastructure
Security architecture, DMZ, virtualization, cloud, honeypots, proxies, IDS and IPS.
Set up a secure small-office Wi-Fi network
MAC filtering, encryption standards and protocols, SSID settings.
Use secure access technologies
ACLs, firewalls, VPNs and network access control (NAC).

domains.name: Endpoint Security Concepts
obj: Describe operating system security
Windows, macOS and Linux features, Defender, host firewalls, CLI and PowerShell, file permissions, privilege escalation.
Use endpoint assessment tools
netstat, nslookup and tcpdump.
Check endpoints against policy
Hardware and software inventory, deployment, backups, compliance (PCI DSS, HIPAA, GDPR), BYOD.
Apply software and hardware updates
Windows Update, application updates, drivers, firmware and patching.
Interpret system logs
Event Viewer, audit logs, system and application logs, syslog, spotting anomalies.
Remove malware
Scanning, reviewing scan logs and remediation.

domains.name: Vulnerability Assessment and Risk Management
obj: Explain vulnerability management
Finding, managing and fixing weaknesses; active and passive reconnaissance; port scanning and automation.
Use threat intelligence to find weaknesses
Vulnerability databases and their limits, CVEs, reports and news, ad hoc vs automated intel, documentation.
Explain risk management
Vulnerability vs risk, ranking risks, mitigation strategies, risk levels, data classification.
Explain disaster recovery and business continuity
DRP vs BCP, backups, and detective, preventive and corrective controls.

domains.name: Incident Handling
obj: Monitor events and know when to escalate
SIEM and SOAR, network monitoring, packet captures, log analysis, suspicious events.
Explain forensics and attack attribution
Cyber Kill Chain, MITRE ATT&CK, Diamond Model, TTPs, evidence handling and chain of custody.
Explain how compliance shapes incident handling
GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, FERPA and FISMA; reporting and notification rules.
Describe incident response
Policy, plan and procedure; the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle.

extras.title: Risk words
rows: A weakness, like an unpatched service.
Someone or something that could use the weakness.
The method or code that actually uses it.
Likelihood times impact. What you rank and fix.

extras.title: Control types
rows: Firewall rule, MFA, a locked door.

extras.title: Attack frameworks
rows: Seven stages from recon to actions on objectives.
A catalog of real attacker tactics and techniques.
Links adversary, capability, infrastructure and victim.

extras.title: Endpoint tools
rows: Every connection and listening port, with the process ID (Windows).
What a name resolves to, and which server answered.
Capture traffic on Linux or macOS, e.g. tcpdump -i eth0 port 53.

method: Use the five areas as your checklist. Cisco gives no weights, so give each one equal time.
Learn the vocabulary cold: risk vs threat vs vulnerability, control types, the IR lifecycle.
Run netstat, nslookup and Event Viewer on your own PC. Capture traffic with Wireshark or tcpdump.
Flashcards for attacks, frameworks, compliance laws and the NIST incident response phases.
Timed 50-minute practice sets. Review every miss and why the other answers were wrong.
tips: 50 minutes goes fast. Cisco exams usually don't let you go back, so answer before you move on.
When asked what to do first, it's usually verify or contain, not wipe or rebuild.
Know the exact difference between vulnerability, threat, exploit and risk. Questions turn on it.
There's no penalty for guessing, so always pick something.

quiz.q: Someone sets up a Wi-Fi hotspot with the same name as the base café's network and captures the logins of people who join it. What is this attack?
o: An evil twin, a rogue access point used for man-in-the-middle
Right. The fake AP imitates a trusted SSID so traffic flows through the attacker.
Denial of service
DoS knocks a service offline. This attack keeps people connected so it can watch them.
Ransomware
Ransomware encrypts files for payment. Nothing is encrypted here.
A botnet
A botnet is a group of infected machines under remote control.

quiz.q: Which control protects INTEGRITY rather than confidentiality?
o: A SHA-256 hash published next to a download so users can check the file wasn't changed
Right. Hashes detect changes, which is integrity.
AES encryption on a laptop's drive
Encryption keeps data secret: confidentiality.
A UPS on the server
Backup power keeps the server running: availability.
Need-to-know file permissions
Limiting who can read files is confidentiality.

quiz.q: A PC keeps receiving ARP replies it never asked for, claiming the gateway's IP now belongs to an unknown MAC address. What is happening?
o: ARP spoofing, to put the attacker in the middle of the PC's traffic
Right. Fake ARP replies poison the cache so traffic for the gateway goes to the attacker first.
DNS amplification
That abuses open DNS resolvers to flood a target. It isn't ARP.
A SYN flood
A SYN flood overwhelms a server with half-open TCP connections.
DHCP starvation
Starvation drains the DHCP pool with fake requests. It doesn't forge ARP replies.

quiz.q: A public web server must be reachable from the internet but must not give attackers a path into the internal network. Where should it go?
o: In a DMZ, a separate segment between two firewall zones
Right. A DMZ exposes the server while firewall rules block it from starting connections inward.
On the internal LAN behind NAT
If the server is compromised, the attacker is already inside.
On the same VLAN as the domain controllers
That puts the most exposed system next to the most valuable ones.
On a honeypot
A honeypot is a decoy to attract attackers, not a place for a real service.

quiz.q: You suspect malware on a Windows PC is calling out. Which command shows active connections with the process ID that owns each one?
o: netstat -ano
Right. -a shows all connections and listening ports, -n keeps numbers, -o adds the process ID. Match the PID in Task Manager.
nslookup
nslookup tests DNS resolution. It doesn't list connections.
ipconfig /all
It shows the PC's own address settings.
tracert
It shows the path to one destination, not what's connected now.

quiz.q: An attacker with a normal user account exploits a flaw in a service that runs as SYSTEM, and can now run commands as SYSTEM. What is this called?
o: Privilege escalation
Right. Going from limited rights to higher rights on the same system is privilege escalation.
Lateral movement
Lateral movement is moving to other systems.
Persistence
Persistence is making sure access survives a reboot or logout.
Reconnaissance
Recon is gathering information before an attack.

quiz.q: Two findings: a critical flaw on a lab PC with no network connection, and a medium flaw on the internet-facing VPN that is being actively exploited worldwide. Which do you fix first?
o: The VPN flaw, because exposure and active exploitation make its real risk higher
Right. Risk is likelihood times impact. A reachable, actively exploited system is far more likely to be hit.
The lab PC, because critical always comes before medium
The severity score ignores exposure. With no network path, that flaw is hard to reach.
Both at the same time, since every flaw is equal risk
Risk ranking exists because time and people are limited.
Neither, until the next patch window
Actively exploited, internet-facing flaws can't wait.

quiz.q: After ransomware, the team restores the file server from last night's offline backup. What type of control is the restore?
o: Corrective
Right. Corrective controls fix things after an incident.
Preventive
Preventive controls stop the incident from happening in the first place.
Detective
Detective controls spot an incident, like an alert or a log review.
Deterrent
Deterrents discourage an attack, like warning banners.

quiz.q: During an investigation, a tech images a suspect laptop's drive. What must be recorded every time that evidence changes hands?
o: Chain of custody
Right. It records who had the evidence, when, and why, so it holds up later.
The recovery time objective
An RTO is a business continuity target, not an evidence record.
The CVSS score
CVSS rates vulnerabilities, not evidence.
The Kill Chain stage
That describes the attack, not how evidence was handled.

quiz.q: In the NIST SP 800-61 lifecycle, isolating an infected PC from the network happens in which phase?
o: Containment, eradication and recovery
Right. Isolating the host is containment: stop the spread first.
Preparation
Preparation is plans, tools and training before anything happens.
Detection and analysis
That's spotting and confirming the incident. Isolation comes next.
Post-incident activity
That's lessons learned after the incident is over.

pbqs.title: Name the threat and pick the fix
pbqs.scenario: Four problems came in this week. For each one, name the threat and pick the control that would have stopped it. Each answer is used once.

rows.req: Hundreds of failed logins overnight against one account on the VPN portal, from many IPs.
rows.why: Password guessing at scale. MFA makes a guessed password useless, and lockout slows the guessing.

rows.req: An unknown Raspberry Pi is plugged into a conference room wall jack and has a network address.
rows.why: Network access control (802.1X) only lets known, authenticated devices onto a port.

rows.req: File shares are being renamed to .locked and a ransom note appears on the server.
rows.why: Ransomware. Offline backups it can't reach let you restore without paying.

rows.req: Users got an email “from the CO” asking them to sign in to a fake leave portal.
rows.why: Phishing. Filtering catches many messages, and training helps people report the rest.

pbqs.title: Read the endpoint and network evidence
pbqs.scenario: Each snippet comes from a different tool. Pick what it shows. Each answer is used once; two choices are distractors.

items.why: Port 4444 is a common backdoor port, and “svch0st” (with a zero) running from Public imitates a real Windows process.
Port 23 is Telnet, which sends everything in clear text, password included. Move to SSH.

items.log:
4625  An account failed to log on.  Account: admin  Source: 10.1.9.40
(57 events in 2 minutes)
items.why: Event 4625 is a failed logon. Dozens in minutes for one account is password guessing.
The gateway's IP points to the same MAC as another host, not the router's real MAC. The ARP cache has been poisoned.
One source trying a thousand ports in seconds is a port scan, mapping what's open.

items.log:
Threat: Trojan:Win32/Wacatac
File: C:\Users\jdoe\Downloads\invoice.exe
Action: Quarantine   Status: Succeeded
items.why: Defender found a trojan and quarantined it. Still check how it arrived and whether anything ran.

keep.text: A CCST earned on or after July 15, 2025 is valid for 5 years. One earned before that date doesn't expire.
keep.after: Renew by passing any current CCST, associate, professional or expert Cisco exam. Continuing education credits don't count for CCST.

keep.text: CCST isn't on the DoD 8140 qualification matrix. On its own it won't qualify you for a coded billet.
keep.after: For cyber work roles, Security+ or CCNA Cybersecurity are on the matrix.
